title: One dust population explains the deep dips and the 4.6 and 12 um excess of the old star Gaia20cdd only if its grains are carbon-rich and 2-7 au from the star; the dust is transient
abstract: Prior campaign studies found that small grains cause the deep dips of the kinematically old K-type star Gaia20cdd and that the star has a 4.6 um (W2) excess. We tested with Mie theory and archival data whether one dust population can cause both. The AllWISE 12 um (W3) detection (S/N 4.8, W3 excess 3.5 +- 1.0 times the photosphere) is probably real: 1.2 percent of 332 similar field stars show one. Radiation pressure does not blow out astrosilicate grains of any size (beta <= 0.47); sub-micron graphite has beta up to 2.5. To make the W2 and W3 excess, small silicate grains must be at 0.04-0.24 au (940-1160 K), where orbits last 27-33 days or less, shorter than the 61-day core of the 2022 dip. Small graphite grains make the excess at 2.1-4.6 au (one star) or 3.1-6.8 au (binary) at about 345 K. This range agrees with the ingress-speed limit and includes the proposed 7.9-8.1 year orbit. Thus only absorbing, carbon-rich grains let one population explain all data; silicate dust needs a transient inner ring or a second population. The dust absorbs 0.9-3.4 percent of the starlight and covers 1-5 percent of the sky seen from the star, against a 10.0 percent (4.9-15.9) time-averaged ZTF r deficit on our line of sight, so the structure is thick (H/r about 0.1-0.5). It is 1e5 to 1e9 times brighter than a steady collisional cascade at 8 Gyr (at least 90 times with extreme parameters), so it is transient, and it needs 3e21 to 1e22 g of new dust per year. The second deep dipper Gaia DR3 2870538750879109504 has no W1 change during its slow optical fade (kappa1 = -0.06 +- 0.04) and no 4.6 um excess in 2014-2024. Limitations: W3 is near the detection limit; spheres, two materials and optically thin emission; no spectra exist. display.caption: Kepler period against orbital radius for Gaia20cdd. Blue: radii where small astrosilicate grains make the W2 + W3 excess; red: the same for small graphite grains. Orange: the 7.9-8.1 year recurrence hypothesis. Green dotted: ingress-speed limits. Horizontal lines: the 61-day core of the 2022 dip, the shortest period that lets that core recur, and the sub-day 2023 event.

Left: chi2 of the W3 excess against the distance of the emitting grains when W2 fixes the amount of dust, for astrosilicate (blue) and graphite (red), one K star (solid) or a K+K binary (dashed). Right: excess against wavelength for the best power-law models with the observed W1 limit, W2 and W3.

Fraction of the sky (seen from the star) that the dust covers, from L_dust/L_star and the absorbed fraction of the grains, for optically thick clumps (filled) and optically thin dust (open). Vertical line and band: the time-averaged ZTF r deficit along our line of sight (2018-2025).
